title: Fourth commandment (CCC 2197–2257)
hook: honor parents, and parents and leaders serve those in their care

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third commandment: Sunday, kept with worship, rest, and time for others. Your line was keep holy the day. What will you set down this Sunday? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

A plastic pill organizer, seven little doors, morning and night. On a weeknight, a woman in her forties fills it for her father. He watches from the doorway, a little embarrassed, a little grateful. Forty years ago, he was the one cutting her grapes in half so she wouldn't choke. Neither of them says anything about it. The roles have quietly turned over. The fourth commandment lives right there, in the turning.
screen: `A PILL ORGANIZER, SEVEN DOORS.` → `ONCE, GRAPES CUT IN HALF.` → `THE ROLES TURN OVER.`

segments.voice: In Exodus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Honour thy father and thy mother." The Catechism says this commandment opens the second part of the law, the part about neighbors, and it starts at home. It calls the family a domestic church. For children, honor means respect, gratitude and, while they live at home, obedience. And it doesn't expire. Grown children, the Catechism says, owe their parents help in old age, sickness, loneliness and distress, as far as they can. The book of Sirach, which the Catechism quotes, asks a son to help his father in his old age and not to grieve him, even if his mind fails. Then the commandment turns around. Parents, the Catechism says, have duties too: to see their children as children of God, to educate them, to be the first to hand on the faith, and to respect their freedom, including their calling in life. Paul writes in Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims: fathers, "provoke not your children to anger." And the circle widens to anyone with authority. The Catechism says those in authority must use it as a service, and Jesus tells his followers that whoever would be great among them must be their servant. Even Jesus, found in the temple at twelve, goes home to Nazareth with Mary and Joseph, and Luke says he "was subject to them." Honor, here, flows up and down at once. Let's look back at the week. Natural law, written in reason. Grace and merit, his gift in us. The precepts, a floor, not a ceiling. Then the commandments begin: God first. Names are holy. Keep holy the day. And today, honor that flows both ways.
screen: `HONOR YOUR FATHER AND MOTHER.` · `GROWN CHILDREN: CARE IN OLD AGE.` · `PARENTS: EDUCATE, RESPECT, SERVE.` · `AUTHORITY AS SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a parent or elder. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent, or an older person who looked after you, even imperfectly. Let one specific thing they did come back: a meal, a ride, a hard word that turned out right. If they're living, plan the words you'll use to thank them for that one thing. If they've died, you can thank them in silence. If the relationship is painful, you can pick another elder instead. If you pray, you can ask God to bless them. The bell holds the time.
Fourth commandment. Honor your father and mother: children honor and care for parents, and parents, and all in authority, serve those in their care. Today's word.
Your line: honor flows both ways. Today, send the thank-you you planned, by call, text or letter. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught to honor and care for their parents throughout life; parents promise at a child's baptism to raise them in the faith, and the Church calls the family a domestic church.

fork.setup: you're twelve. after three days of searching, your worried parents find you in the temple among the teachers. you've told them you must be about your Father's business. what next?
options: stay in the temple; your work matters more.
go home to Nazareth with them, and be subject to them.
send them home and follow later.
fork.reveal: in Luke 2, Jesus goes down with Mary and Joseph to Nazareth and was subject to them.

trapdoor: what you thought: obey your parents.
what it means: lifelong honor and care for parents, and parents and every authority serving those in their care.
what a scholar hears: the first commandment of the second tablet, the domestic church, and authority as service.
